tagline.text: A riverside market since 1851 in Quiapo, known for palabok and halo-halo

location.label: Location
location.text: Carlos Palanca Street, Quiapo, Manila (on the Pasig River beside Quezon Bridge)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (the November–May dry season is more comfortable)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱200~600 (snacks and a meal per person)

children.text: Quinta Market is Manila's best-known public market, built by the Spanish colonial government in 1851 and reopened in a new building in 2017. It is a good starting point for a Quiapo food crawl, with fish, vegetable and side-dish stalls plus famous palabok and halo-halo.

Quinta Market is a public market on Carlos Palanca Street in Quiapo, Manila, right beside the Pasig River. It is also called Quiapo Market, and since 2017 its official name has been Quinta Market and Fishport. The name "quinta" is said to come from a word meaning a country villa by the river.

The market's history goes back to 1851. It was built by the Spanish colonial government with money left to the city of Manila by Francisco Carriedo. An earthquake in 1863 badly damaged it, it was rebuilt in 1878, and around 1900 it was replaced by a steel building that opened in October 1901. It was once Manila's central market and a major source of the city's market revenue, but it declined in the 2000s as department stores in Makati and Quezon City drew shoppers away and congestion and poor hygiene added to the problems.

A 2014 ordinance allowed public-private joint ventures, Quinta became the first market chosen for rebuilding, and demolition began in July 2015 amid protests from vendors. The new two-storey building opened on April 19, 2017, at a reported cost of about ₱150 million. The ground floor holds a market with room for about 360 stalls, the second floor is a parking garage for about 100 vehicles, and the complex also has a food court, a ferry terminal and free Wi-Fi. The building is owned by the City of Manila and is reportedly operated by Marketlife Management and Leasing Corporation under a 25-year joint venture. About 279 vendors were registered at the reopening, and in December of that year a vegetable section stocked with produce from Benguet and a Jollibee branch are said to have opened. Street vendors around the market had long caused congestion, and the city cleared many of them in 2017, though stalls sometimes creep back along the edges today.

For travelers, Quinta's appeal lies less in sights than in seeing ordinary Manila's food and market life up close. Restaurants in and around the market serve Filipino home cooking such as palabok, puto and dinuguan, and it pairs well with Quiapo Church for a half-day outing. Keep in mind that this is not a photo spot or a tourist market but a working market where locals do their shopping. Go to watch everyday life, such as shoppers picking side dishes, vendors cleaning fish and office workers eating lunch, rather than expecting showy attractions, and you will enjoy it more.

The building reopened in 2017, and the ground floor is divided into dry goods and wet goods sections. The aisles are more orderly than before, but the bustle of a traditional market remains, so treat it as a look at how a local day begins. The building is said to have CCTV, air-conditioned restrooms and free Wi-Fi, but conditions vary over time, so keep your expectations modest.

Pastora Special Palabok inside the market was named among Manila's best by the Manila Bulletin in 2014. Palabok, rice noodles topped with shrimp sauce, crushed chicharon and boiled egg, is a signature dish at many stalls around the market. Wikivoyage lists Pastora Special Palabok's hours as daily 10 AM to 6 PM. Hours can change, so check locally.

A story says that the Philippines' signature dessert, halo-halo, started in this area. Some accounts instead trace it to shaved ice brought by Japanese settlers, so the origin is not settled, but it is a source of local pride. Try a bowl at a restaurant near the market.

In small eateries in and around the market you can see Filipino home cooking such as pancit, menudo, puto and dinuguan sold by the plate. It is a good way to sample several dishes in small portions. Dishes are served from trays, so you can simply point to what you want, and if it is your first time, follow the longest line.

As the name Fishport suggests, there is a fish section, and the market also has a terminal linked to the Pasig River ferry. Ferry operations change, so check the latest announcements before you visit.

blocks.title: Ilalim ng Tulay under Quezon Bridge

children.text: The "Ilalim ng Tulay" (under the bridge) area beneath Quezon Bridge has clusters of shops selling furniture, woodwork, handicrafts and souvenirs, where bargaining is part of the fun. Carlos Palanca Street also has many costume and prop shops. Large items such as furniture are hard to carry home as luggage, so small crafts and souvenirs are more realistic.
Quinta is connected on foot to Quiapo Church, Carriedo Street and Quezon Boulevard. Around the market you can see downtown Manila daily life up close, with vendors and pedestrians mixed together.
Get off at LRT-1 Carriedo Station and walk along Carriedo Street toward Quiapo Church. Take a short look inside the church, then come out onto Quezon Boulevard.
Before crossing Quezon Bridge, turn into Carlos Palanca Street and arrive at Quinta Market. Walk once around the ground floor and get a feel for the fish, vegetable and dry goods sections.
Have a snack at a palabok stall or food area inside the market. Portions and prices differ by stall, so check the price list first.
Head out under Quezon Bridge to browse the furniture, crafts and souvenir shops, and bargain if something catches your eye.
Walk through the Quiapo street food lanes or finish with halo-halo, then return to your hotel by taxi or LRT-1.
The market is liveliest in the morning. Some shops may close after lunch, so it is best to go in the morning.

items.title: Quiapo half-day extended
items.subtitle: Market, church and street food together

children.text: Start from LRT-1 Doroteo Jose or Carriedo Station and look around Quiapo Church and the surrounding streets first.
At Quinta Market, walk the ground floor and compare the fish section with the vegetable section.
Try light dishes such as palabok and pancit, and buy drinking water.
Walk under Quezon Bridge and along Carlos Palanca Street to look at the costume and prop shops.
Finish lunch with Quiapo street food or halo-halo, then take a Grab to your next stop.
In the hot months of March to May, cut down on midday outdoor movement and plan generous breaks inside the market and restaurants.
From central Manila (Malate, Ermita and so on) take LRT-1 and get off at Carriedo Station or Doroteo Jose Station. From Carriedo Station it is about a 15–20 minute walk past Quiapo Church to Quinta.
City buses and jeepneys stop below Carriedo Station and on Quezon Boulevard in front of Quiapo Church. Routes change often, so confirm locally.
Quiapo is very congested, so avoiding rush hours makes getting around much easier.
From Makati or BGC, Grab or a taxi is convenient. Traffic around Quiapo can be heavy and slow, so allow extra time.
Setting the destination to Quinta Market (Carlos Palanca Street) is the most accurate choice.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), go by taxi or Grab; depending on traffic it can take around 1 hour. Check the fare locally.

Quinta Market can be visited year-round, and as an indoor market it can be explored even in the rain. However, the surrounding street stalls and the area under Quezon Bridge get muddy and crowded when it rains.

The best time of day is early morning until just before lunch. Wikivoyage gives the market's hours as 4 AM to 9 PM, while another guide says 5:30 AM to 7 PM, so sources differ. Hours vary by shop, so check locally.

There are not many upscale hotels around Quiapo, so it is easier to stay in Malate, Ermita, Intramuros or Makati and visit as a day trip. Staying overnight in Quiapo itself is not recommended for ordinary travelers.

There are plenty of places to eat in and around Quinta. Pastora Special Palabok inside the market, Palabok d'e Tisoy under Quezon Bridge and Jolli Dada's Eatery are well known, but their hours and prices change often. Lines can be long at mealtimes, so go a little early. If hygiene worries you, pick busy stalls with fast turnover and bring your own bottled water.

The food court inside the market and chain outlets such as Jollibee are alternatives if street food feels like too much. At local home-cooking eateries it is normal to order rice plus one or two dishes, which keeps the cost and the risk low, and pancit and puto also work well as snacks. Choose bottled water or canned drinks. Children and anyone with a sensitive stomach should avoid drinks with ice and raw food.
Quiapo is known for pickpockets and begging. Keep your wallet and phone in a front pocket or an inner bag pocket, and leave valuables at your hotel.
Carry cash in small bills. Small shops often will not take large notes or lack change.
Order one plate at a time and move between several shops to sample the food.
Ask vendors for permission before taking their photo.
If touts approach you with goods, smile, decline and keep walking.
The floor inside the market can be wet, so wear non-slip shoes.
Combining a visit with Quiapo Church on the same day is efficient. Fridays are especially crowded in front of the church, so allow plenty of time.
Opening hours and market rules can change, so check the latest announcements.
The market gets going from around 4–5 in the early morning, so go early if you want to see fresh goods, and mid-morning is easier if you mainly want to eat.
If you find jeepneys or buses hard to use, setting a Grab destination to Quinta Market from the start is the way to avoid getting lost.
Quiapo is known even within Manila for its many pickpockets. Keep your belongings secure and move on before dark.
In crowded places wear your bag in front, and do not hold your phone out on the street for long.
Street stalls around the market shift location with enforcement, so older information may no longer match.
Roads around the market can flood when it rains, so check the weather.
Bargaining too hard or taking photos carelessly can lead to disputes, so be polite.
Avoid traveling alone late at night and use Grab or a trustworthy taxi.
If you need to withdraw cash, use ATMs at LRT stations or inside shopping malls rather than roadside ATMs in Quiapo.
